item.research_question: How do the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powders evolve during mechanical alloying, and what are the resulting coating properties when deposited via atmospheric plasma spraying?
item.material_system: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy (equimolar mixture of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Si elemental powders)
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying in a high-energy planetary ball mill (QM-3SP2) at 300 r·min−1, ball-to-powder weight ratio 10:1, powder loading 90 g for 5, 10, 20, and 30 h; coating deposition via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using 10 h milled powder, 45 kW arc power, 100 mm spray distance, 200 mm·s−1 traverse speed, with argon primary gas (0.4 MPa) and nitrogen secondary gas (0.3 MPa)
item.test_conditions: Room temperature microhardness testing (200 g load, 10 s dwell); wear testing using a Si3N4 ball (Φ 5 mm) at 5 N load, 573 r·min−1 rotation speed, 5 mm friction radius, for 30 min; XRD (2θ 20–90°, 3°·min−1); FESEM and TEM characterization
key_findings: Particle size first increased then decreased with milling time; at 10 h, a narrow peak range from several micrometers to about 50 μm was obtained.
At 10 h milling, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed with an average grain size of 11.7 nm and lattice strain of about 0.73%.
After plasma spraying, the lamellar structure inside a single particle disappeared, and an ordered BCC phase was detected while Si diffraction peaks vanished.
Transmission electron microscopy revealed nanometer crystalline grains with a grain size of about 30 nm in the APS coating.
The coating exhibited an average microhardness of 612 ± 41 HV.
The volume wear rate of the coating was (0.38 ± 0.08) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, approximately half that of a previously studied AlCoCrFeNiTi coating.
Wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, tribo-oxidation wear, and slight abrasion wear.
The coefficient of friction reached a steady state average of 0.57 ± 0.02 after an initial running-in stage of 6 min.
item.mechanism: During mechanical alloying, plastic deformation and cold welding dominate initially, increasing particle size, followed by work hardening and fracture which reduce particle size and refine the lamellar structure. During plasma spraying, high temperatures cause melting and elemental rearrangement, leading to the disappearance of the lamellar structure, formation of an ordered BCC phase, and dissolution of Si elemental peaks. The high hardness and formation of hard tribofilms contribute to the coating's good wear resistance.
item.limitations: The text notes that unmelted and semi-melted particles were present in the coating due to stochastic heating, and that limited interlamellar bonding ratio (less than one third) in thermally sprayed coatings can deteriorate mechanical properties.
item.future_work: The authors state the coating is promising for use in abrasive environments in industries such as petroleum, power, and mining, implying future application in these sectors.
quotes: At the milling time of 10 h, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed.
An average microhardness of 612 ± 41 HV was obtained.
The coating showed good wear resistance, with a volume wear rate of 0.38 ± 0.08 × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1
